children: Dalian iron ore futures fell to their lowest level in more than 16 months on Monday after weak Chinese economic data reinforced concerns about steel demand in the world's largest consumer of the steelmaking ingredient.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
dropped 3.28% to 648 yuan ($97.15) a metric ton, its weakest level since July 2, 2025.
The benchmark December iron ore (SZZFZ6) on the Singapore Exchange was 2.71% lower at $88 a ton, as of 0700 GMT, touching its lowest since September 2024.
China's industrial output grew 4.8% year-on-year in October, missing a Reuters poll forecast of 5.3% and slowing from 5.5% in September, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed.

Property investment tumbled 21.6% in the first 10 months from a year earlier, worsening from a 20.6% decline recorded in January-September. New construction starts by floor area fell 24.4% and property sales by floor area declined 13.7%.
China's crude steel output fell 3.8% in October from September to its lowest so far this year, weighed down by subdued home demand, falling exports and persistently thin margins.

Average daily hot metal output, a gauge of iron ore demand, fell 3,700 tons week-on-week to 2.3 million tons among 247 steel mills last week, while the blast furnace capacity utilisation rate fell 0.14 percentage points to 86.48%, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.
Steel mills are increasing maintenance during the off-season, keeping iron ore fundamentals under pressure, analysts from broker Ningzheng Futures said in a note.
Iron ore inventory at major Chinese ports rose 1.09% week-on-week to 156.2 million tons on Friday, data from consultancy Steelhome showed.
